p1: There is a gesture most of us never think about. You pick something up, you put it in the back of a car, you close the door, and some time later it is somewhere else. Venice has spent this year teaching us how much that gesture hides.
p2: Running a pavilion at the Biennale is, in large part, a problem of moving things. Plaster, pigment, timber, foam, tools, crates of finished work: everything the studio uses has to arrive at Tesa 41, at the far end of the Arsenale, and almost nothing arrives the way it would anywhere else.
h2-back-seat: A city without a back seat
p3: There are no streets here in the sense we mean. There are canals, and there are bridges, and a bridge is a staircase. A courier van stops at Piazzale Roma or Tronchetto, and from there every parcel continues by boat, by hand, or by both. Pallets come up the canals and are lifted ashore by crane. Everything else goes on a hand truck, one box at a time, up one side of a bridge and down the other, and then again at the next one.
fig-crane.caption: Crates landed on the Arsenale quay, the crane still at work
p4: A delivery that would take an afternoon in Los Angeles becomes a small expedition. It needs a time window, a person on the dock, a call to the right office, the right boat at the right tide. A missed handover is not an inconvenience; it is another day. We have learned the names of the bridges between the vaporetto stop and our door the way you learn the stops on a commute, by how many steps each one has.
fig-campo.caption: Across a campo with the morning's boxes
p5: What has surprised us is how instructive this is. The car, the truck, the forklift have made weight almost abstract. We stopped feeling what things weigh because we stopped carrying them. Venice gives it back. Every object has to be lifted by someone, held by someone, set down by someone. You start to think about a sculpture not only as a form but as a load: how many hands it needs, how it turns on a narrow stair, where it can rest.
p6: The city is ancient, and it is stubborn about it. It does not make room for the conveniences we take for granted, and so it slows everything down to the speed of a body. In that sense Venice is less an obstacle than a teacher. It is a long, daily meditation on gravity.
fig-calle.caption: Down a narrow calle, sharing the stairs
p7: We also owe our visitors an honest account of the summer. Visa requirements meant that Zadik and Aram had to travel to Armenia to put the proper paperwork in place. The process took most of July and August, and while we were away the pavilion was not able to do what it set out to do: to be a working studio, producing work in public. That was a real loss for us, and we know for some of you who came by expecting to see the studio in motion.
p8: The good news is that we are back. Since the first of September the studio has been returning to full production: the tools are running again, materials are arriving, and the blocks are being cast, finished and arranged at Tesa 41.
fig-unloading.caption: Materials arriving again at Tesa 41, the last few metres by trolley
p9: And the summer has left us with an idea. All year we have carried things to the work. We have begun to wonder what it would mean to carry the work itself: to take it out of the pavilion and into the city, by hand, over the same bridges, at the same pace. We will say more about that soon.
closing: For now, the studio is open again, Tuesday to Sunday. Come and see it working.
